He says his address was in Vojvodina, so they couldn't trace him in Banja Luka, and he says that he was arrested in August 1992. Sanski Most is not important, but it says here that he was charged, but General Milan Uzelac, the commander of the Yugoslav People's Forces of the corps of Banja Luka in the Yugoslav People's Army intervened, and he was released, which means that Uzelac knew very well where he was, and he was released without any documents. That meant that he could not leave the town, which simply wasn't true. I don't know what the rest of the document has been translated, but if it hasn't been, I can read it, because everything seems very odd. He says he was arrested in August 1992, that he had been in town for 15 days, and that on the eve of the attack against the municipality that took place on the 12th of May, he talked about defence with Sabic, Kljucanin and Osmancevic. Now, the 19th of May certainly precedes August 1992, of course. He met with the Muslims already then - this was in Banja Luka - and I believe at that time it was simply not possible. And why am I saying this? I'm saying this because of the following paragraph, which is paragraph 13.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, you have to read, because we don't have a translation.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He says: "This meant that I was free," this has been translated, "but that I could not leave town." And I continue, and I quote: "I stayed in town for 15 days after that. It was only on the eve of the attack on the municipality which took place on the 19th of May, 1992," and we know that the war was already raging in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time, and I continue quoting from his book: "I talked to Sabic, Kljucanin and Osmancevic about defence. I didn't know whether anything had been organised. I didn't know how many men they had, where they were." And he says that the talks took place two days before the Chetnik attack on the town. How did Chetniks attack Banja Luka? I'm not clear on that, and I'm also not clear how come he was arrested in August 1992, and then he says after that he spent another 15 days in town, and so on and so forth. Let's move on, and then you will see what happened next. The arrival in Travnik, that's on page 13 in the Bosniak version.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: 3D41-0090 in the English version, and 3D33-0344 in the Croatian version of the text.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look here. The gentleman, who is in Banja Luka, talks about the organisation of defence, and then on the 13th of January, 1993, he appears in Travnik. He reported to the personnel officer in the barracks. Thus, in the barracks in Travnik, which had been abandoned by the JNA, the HVO troops and the BiH Army troops were billeted. He volunteered, and he said that he could be a foot soldier or a commander. He said that he was a lieutenant-colonel by rank and that his complete personal documentation was in his brief-case. Before that, he said that his documents had been taken away from him. He went to Visoko. He met with Cuskic, Mahmuljin and Hadzihasanovic there. He said the barracks did not look like a military premises. He was given a task to organise three battalions. And then somebody accused him of being a Communist and asked him why he was there, and his reply was that that person, that soldier, could not replace him and that Alagic could, in turn, replace that other person in his place. Your Honours, it is absolutely unclear what happened between May or August 1992 until the 13th of January, 1993, what Mr. Alagic was doing during all that time and where he was during all that time. Obviously, he did not write this in his book. However, if somebody spends six months under a fierce attack of the JNA and Chetniks against his people, he was hiding somewhere, unless, once he was released by Uzelac, he did not start working for the JNA, and you will see why. Six months, only the 13th of January, he reported in order to help the defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and he says that before that, he could not leave town. If he could not leave town in May, then - and I'm talking about May 1992 - then in January 1993, it's absolutely unclear how he was even alive. Let's go to page 14.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Just a moment. 3D41-0091. Croatian, 3D33-0345.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now look how this functioned. He says that when he arrived, those were the first elements of the preparations for a serious war against the Chetniks. It seems that before that, they did not deal with the Chetniks at all. And he goes on to say at that time Cuskic returned from his holiday that he had spent in Rijeka. So Cuskic, the army commander, was in Croatia, spending his holidays in Rijeka. They agree to establish the Bosanska Krajina OG group, and that OG group would incorporate four brigades; the 7th, the 17th, the 27th and the 37th. It was only then that they established the brigades. What they did before that and who was defending the area from the Chetniks, I leave to the Trial Chamber to conclude. And now look at this: An order to establish the OG Group Bosanska Krajina was issued on the 27th February. Thus, on the 27th February, 1992 -- that's 3, madam. Rasim Imamovic had arrived from Zagreb with an order to establish the Motorised Banja Luka Brigade headquartered in Zagreb, or rather its command would be headquartered in Zagreb, which means that the refugees from Banja Luka, who ran for their dear life, Muslims, had the seat of their command in Zagreb; and they issued the order to use all the men that would become a motorised brigade, and thus they established the 27th, composed of some refugees from Kotor Varos, and it was only then, as he says, some orders were issued, but they were not implemented, and these were the beginnings of the BiH Army, and in that area that army would show its strength exclusively, or predominantly, on the HVO. And now let's move on to page 15.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Just a question before that. You mentioned Mehurici. Where is Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is -- it is in Central Bosnia. This was the central base of the Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. And now the page that you are moving to now, I have not written it down. It is 3D, in Croatian, 33-0346, and in the English version it is 3D41-0091.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He elaborates here and says that there was the Jajce syndrome. He says that people had to have the idea restored into their heads that they would be returning home, because the entire region of Krajina, and I mean, Your Honours, the west and north part of Bosnia-Herzegovina from Banja Luka in the direction of Croatia. And he says that people were fleeing to Europe, across Croatia, and they were considering the transfer of some units to Bihac. The HVO printed papers as travel documents. It says here that the HVO officers, which at that time still cooperated with us, were holding it against him for organising m mobilisation. I don't know where he draws the right to proclaim mobilisation. And, second of all, the mobilisation was proclaimed by Mr. Izetbegovic, i.e., the Presidency. And he says that he concentrated units in Travnik. He says that he had brought in the 305th Jajce, a brigade that was composed of the refugees from Jajce; Muslims. And now, please, he says that he was visited by Ambassador Thebault, the Vance-Owen Plan was already topical. And now, Your Honours, look what he says to Thebault, and I quote: "This is where this plan is going to fall through, Mr. Thebault." And he also says to him: "This is where Herceg-Bosna is going to fall onto its knees." And he also says that the joint barracks in Travnik, he was not going to share with the HVO. And he says very determinedly two militaries cannot share a barracks, two flags cannot be on that building. He said to the commander of the HVO, You are going to leave the barracks, whatever happened later on concerning the arrest of the people in the barracks in Travnik. And he says the commander of the area says very neatly, and he continued. He says that he was unknown. His successes were not known to Milosevic and Tudjman. Milosevic and Tudjman did not know anything about him. Can you imagine the arrogant vanity of a JNA officer who's hiding in Banja Luka and talks to Uzelac and makes God knows what kind of arrangements with him; and Tudjman and Milosevic knew of him, and that's why he was successful in his attacking the HV, robbing them of any right to existence unless they do what he said, because, as he found -- as he found later, Tudjman and Milosevic had split Bosnia-Herzegovina, and Alagic - they don't know anything about him - he is an enigma for him, and that's why he's going to do things differently and he's going to defy their plans. I believe everything is clear, the misery of this way of thinking, but I'll skip all that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: There may be a miss -- you may have misspoken, or an error in the translation, perhaps, on line 11. You explained that this is why he was successful in his attacking the HV. Should it not read "HVO"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, you have mentioned for the second time Uzelac. Who was Uzelac?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Uzelac was the commander of the Banja Luka Corps. Uzelac was the commander of the Banja Luka Corps of the Yugoslav People's Army, and later on, I believe, of the Army of Republika Srpska. I don't know the rest of his career, but he was the most important Serb in that area. He released him from prison. For the next six and seven months, nobody knew what he was doing, and then Travnik comes, and you see what he says about Travnik. And this is, Your Honours, something we don't have any direct evidence about, but these things show that they infiltrated into the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Serbs infiltrated into the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina people who were working for them during the course of events and who, amongst other factors, caused the BiH Army to provoke a conflict and attack the HVO not only in Central Bosnia but also in Vakuf, Konjic and Mostar. And now can we go on to page 18, where he develops the thesis.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: It is 3D33-0348 in Croatian, and in English this is 3D41-0092.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Firstly, he provides an explanation to justify his actions. He says that the Croats -- or, rather, that the Chetniks had managed to reach their political positions and that the Croats instilled political structures in the area that should have been Croatian. There were a lot of more Muslims there, and at that time Croats didn't play -- which you can see from the stories of the people who came to see Franjo Tudjman. They were already in an inferior position, much inferior. And then he says that the heads of the HDZ were transformed into the commanders of the HVO, and then he goes on to say he was of the opinion that for the strategic situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina, not only in Central Bosnia, and he arrived at a conclusion that only a wedge in the centre of Bosnia could have broken their grip, and when he says "their grip," he means the Croats and the HVO. The overall situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina, according to the ideas of Commander Alagic, who is in command of four very strong brigades of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina would become clear, not after an attack against the Chetniks, the Army of Republika Srpska; he's rather going to use a wedge in order to break from the grip of the HVO. This is what he plans.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but I will have to correct the transcript, although the general is really doing his best to speak slowly. At page 40 [as interpreted], line 11, the general did not say Herzegovina would become clear, but would become resolved. So the general didn't say that the situation would be clear, but that the situation would be resolved.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think we have to correct the correction. That was not page 40, but page 60 that you referred to.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely, that's correct. I said "60."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And that's not what Praljak is saying. That's what Alagic is saying, and that's why we have to read all those words very calmly. A, the whole of the strategic situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina would be resolved by breaking the grip of the HVO. That was very important to do, and he says, We actually managed to do that later. And at the time of writing, he believes that in the areas where he attacked the HVO and where he achieved his goals, partially, of course, that the definitive division of Bosnia and Herzegovina was prevented. Serbs, nothing, 70 percent of the territory, nothing that was occupied. He's only interested in the HVO. And by defeating the HVO in Central Bosnia, he prevented the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Your Honours, this is the concept that the high-ranking officers in the BH Army had, and this was written here quite specifically, who attacked whom in Central Bosnia, who harboured what intentions, and who thought what. Further, he goes on to say that the Operative Group Bosnian Krajina is an example of the finest troops of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and he specifically speaks about two brigades, the 7th Muslim and the 17th Krajina Brigade. And he goes on to say that they operated in Travnik, Zenica, and Kacuni --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters remark, could Mr. Praljak please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the intention of the enemy, of course. The enemy is a reference to the HVO, to take the Lasva valley, Travnik, Vitez, the Lasva, not the Busovaca area. And this mobile prevented this intention and now he goes on to say --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters remark, the interpreters cannot hear Mr. Praljak because he's not really speaking into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, please, the interpreter is asking you to speak to the microphone, and of course speak more slowly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. So, Your Honour, they attacked Sebesic. You can see they had hundreds of orders for the attack. The HVO has no attack orders, apart from some minor tactical movements or what is called the active defence. He says that they won a victory, and our tactics, he say, consists -- he says consisted of infiltrating elements of our forces into the rear and then creating conditions for attacks from a circular base. The people from -- the guys from Sebesic later on fought in the Prozor area. I know those guys. Sebesic is deep behind this line. It's a place that is between Vakuf and Travnik. And apart from cleaning up and the attack to take this road, there's no other purpose, apart from defeating the HVO. Let us move on to page 21.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I have a question, Mr. Praljak. You have said that there were hundreds -- or that, We had or we could see hundreds of attack orders from the ABiH. I do not see them. Can you explain where we see them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this case, Your Honour, we have seen at least a hundred orders from the BH Army for attacks, from Mostar to Konjic, Vares; and they are on the record, where it says quite explicitly an attack order. In the Neretva-93 offensive, dozens and dozens of such orders.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, I'm sorry. Before we go on to this page, as regards Sebesic, what was the importance of Sebesic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It afforded control of the roads. It was a dominant point.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. The page is 3D41-0092 in English. And 3D33-0349, that's in the Croatian language.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this decision for him to take the Bosnian Posavina Operative Group was taken at a meeting in Plave Vode in Travnik. That was their command that I went to often, and I knew where it was. And Hadzihasanovic gave him some other units, 306, 325, 312, all those brigades. I don't want to now list them all. And then they were to be joined by the 27th Brigade, which was in the process of forming, and 75th Jajce Brigade.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters remark, we did not really hear the number.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now we can see the cynicism at play. This is where it starts. So expecting the attack of the HVO on Travnik, after he had already expelled them from the barracks, and after at least -- the units that were at least seven times as strong as the small Travnik Brigade, but at any rate, he says, Expecting the attack on Travnik, we have already deployed our forces in secret, not only in the town but in the entire area. On Vilenica, we had our forces behind the HVO back without them being aware of it. And then he goes on to say we -- that they were ready to take positions facing the Chetniks that were, of course, held by the HVO, but once they attacked the HVO, the HVO would abandon the lines facing Chetniks to defend itself, and then they would take those lines. And then he goes on to say, And that is why when the city was mopped up at around 1300 hours, I got onto a white mare, and that's what winners do. The victors ride on white horses. And so on and so forth. So they prepared the attack in secrecy. They deployed the units behind the HVO backs. They did not hold the lines against the Chetniks. They cleaned up the town, they expelled the population. They captured a certain number of people, killed some of them. And this is stated explicitly by a person who was in charge of these events, who participated in those events, a general of the BH Army, Alagic. Let us move on. Page 26 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I would like to say something.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Sorry. Before you go to other pages, I would like to ask you about page 7 in the English text, and which is actually the page 30, 3-0, of the original text, and here is an important point which I would like to raise. On page 30 of the original text, and page 7 here, the headline says that, and I quote: "Croatia sent 13 of its own brigades to Gornji Vakuf, Prozor and Jablanica." When I read it first, I thought that probably there is a mistake, if the author would like to speak about the 13th, that is, and not the 13 brigades. And when I checked the original, it is being said here, and I quote, and I am sorry for my pronunciation, that "Hrvatska in Gornji Vakuf, Prozor, Jablanica [B/C/S spoken]." So, anyway, we speak -- or they speak about 13 brigades of Croatia. Now, a few days ago, as we recall, there had been a discussion and exchange of views on the facts -- on the alleged facts, if there were any Croatian official units in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and of course you spoke about this question. So now how would you explain this assertion that Croatia had 13 of its own brigades in that area, that is, Gornji Vakuf, Prozor and Jablanica? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's quite simple, Your Honour Judge Prandler. It is simply an insane lie. Thirteen brigades of the Croatian Army liberated -- well, that's what I wanted to get to. I didn't mean to skip that, but now we're talking about 1994, when they talk about Here and so on. And as I've already told you, I was there in 1994, although the Prosecution did not mention that. I was there around Here. Well, I admit to that, and they can write this down and ask me about it. Thirteen brigades of the HV -- of the Croatian Army defeated Martic's army and liberated Krajina. And when -- well, they liberated Bihac. And when they headed towards Banja Luka, it was a very strict order from Franjo Tudjman and, in turn, from the Americans, Stop the troops from inflicting a decisive defeat on the Bosnian Serbs. Thirteen brigades of the Croatian Army would have gone through to Tuzla in three days, but those lies served only to fluff up his own glory, because he faced 13 brigades of the Croatian Army and yet he defeated them all. But Alagic says, for himself, that he's so cunning because Milosevic and Tudjman couldn't really grasp what he was all about. Can you get into the mind of this man, this man who is hiding in Banja Luka and who is trying to get some arrangements? And now he believes that Tudjman and Milosevic are really thinking about him, but he managed to slip through, and he managed to prevent the division of Bosnia and Herzegovina by defeating the HVO in Central Bosnia. He does not speak about any actions against Chetniks in his book, not a single one, because he's not interested in that. His group, the 7th, the 17th, and all the other brigades, he did not take this group and lead it towards Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I hate to interrupt you, but for me, your answer is enough. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, if we use the assumption that late General Alagic is telling the truth, that there are 13 brigades, it is an important armed forces and theoretically these brigades, which moved, must have moved along with orders. You know, there must be some evidence. You can't move 13 brigades without physicians and logistics and so forth and so on. So if he's really telling the truth, in the archives and in the documents of the Croatian Army, we must find evidence of this. You had a very senior position in the Croatian Army, so what can you tell us about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, the same thing. Well, let the Prosecution show any order to any Croatian brigade at that time, in that area. Thirteen brigades of the Croatian Army, that's almost 30.000 soldiers, 30.000 soldiers. 30.000 soldiers, in addition to all of those who were there, well, that's -- these are columns that are hundreds of kilometres long. A brigade that is moving in echelons, it's hundreds of kilometres long. This is such a bare-faced stupid lie, because you can have an intelligent lie. If he mentioned just a brigade, well, then perhaps you can work around that, but if somebody is really talking nonsense and just blathering on and lying, but when he's also stupid, then he says 13 brigades, 30.000 soldiers, that's the 13 brigades of the Croatian Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, so we've got one part of the book that the general is tendering, which he contends is a lie. Now I'd like to take us back to another part of the book which he wants the Trial Chamber to accept as true because evidently it suits his case, and I want to get the time-frame for that. This is -- I'm looking at page 6 of the English translation. I think it's page 21 of the book. At least that's what the translation indicates. The general was talking about this incident or this text in which it's written about the 306th and the 325th and the 312th, et cetera, Brigades, and the decision to try to take the Operative Zone Bosanska Krajina. That's something the general was talking about a couple of minutes ago, and how Alagic evidently redeployed the ABiH units away from the Serb positions and put them in a position to face the HVO. What's the time-frame, if I could ask, when all that is said to have occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These attacks on Sebesic were in the spring, February or March. Travnik was cleared up, and we know that for sure. Petkovic, stand up and tell us. I can't remember the date exactly. If you know about that, I think Their Honours will let you get to your feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not without the Judges' permission.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I meant with the Judges' permission. When Travnik was cleared up, it was 1993, in May or June. That's correct. Now, what Judge Prandler was saying about 1994, those were -- there was fighting in January 1994, when they attempted to break through again at Vakuf. And, Your Honours, and gentlemen of the Prosecution, I state again that I was there again as a volunteer and I took part in that, and there were no Croatian forces over there at that time. We achieved certain tactical steps in advance, and I took part in them, and I can enumerate: Ciganske Livade, Zavisce, Skarina Glava, Here, and perhaps one more that I can't quite remember just now. I came here to tell the truth, and I shall tell the truth. So he cleared up Travnik in May or the beginning of June 1993, but that is easily established if we look at the documents that we have at our disposal. And I'd like to look at page 26, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. We will take a look at page 26 after the break. It's time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I wish to apologise to everyone. I have another engagement in another country, which will force me to leave after the break. I will read up, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, before we continue, just to correct something it says in the transcript on page 67, line 5. When you were speaking about the length of the deployment and development of 13 brigades and one brigade, it says in the transcript that one brigade moves hundreds of kilometres.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. We have had the problem -- or, rather, how much an infantry or armoured brigade, when it marches in echelon, what length of a route this occupies. First of all, the brigade doesn't always move in an echelon, in echelon formation, but two echelons. And then I drew a diagram and proposed to Their Honours that a brigade moving along the road goes for about 45, 50 -- takes up 45 to 50 kilometres of vehicles, men, and everything else that a brigade is composed of. So if you have 13 brigades, well, in Vakuf I can't speak about anything so stupid. Especially there's that report of mine which I sent from Rama and Uskoplje to myself, I addressed it to myself in 1993, when I asked the others to tell me exactly how many men we have up at the front-line. And from that document, which has already been admitted into evidence, and it was written during the war, it's quite clear what forces I had. And in 1993, I was leading the defence of Uskoplje and defending them from the BH Army, the manpower and strength I had, and it's below my logical dignity to talk about 13 brigades of the Croatian Army in that area; of 30.000 soldiers, that would be.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. That was for the record. As far as I know, we left off discussing page 26 of the book, which is 3D41-0093 in English and 3D33-0350 in Croatian.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He goes on to explain the war in Central Bosnia, and he says that the decisive moment was the break through in the Krizancevo Selo, which was on the 22nd or 23rd of December, 1993. One has to note here that about 70 people were killed not in combat. Those people were killed in Krizancevo Selo. There's a report to that effect by the English intelligence officers, and there are some other documents. And he says that after that, the Croats were forced to sign a cease-fire agreement. As far as I know, and General Petkovic will know even better than me, that at least such -- ten such cease-fire agreements were signed, and we adhered to them. And this is how he explains why he did not liberate Vitez, liberate Vitez. He says that this is due to the fact that he was left there as a strategic valve, that Vitez was left there as a strategic valve. If they had taken Vitez, arms and the rest of the things would have stopped coming from Croatia. And he says there was a shortage of everything, food and everything else, and that was one strategic problem, and that Croatia would perhaps have changed its position. And Croatia unfortunately, if I may say so, did not change its position after all of the operations and all-out aggression. And he says that he was afraid he would not be able to control the troops after what had happened in Ahmici and Stupni Do. Krizancevo Selo, Uzdol, Grabovica, and all the others where the BH Army killed over 1100 Croats outside combat, he doesn't say a word about that. So much about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Our next page is 30 --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but here I've already answered that question. Truth be told, at that time General Roso was in command of the HVO, and I said that I -- after having left the position as the commander of the Main Staff of the HVO, because of further attacks after the cease-fires had been signed, there was a cease-fire agreement which was signed in October 1993. After the offensive by the BH Army, Neretva-93 was stopped. They did not stop attacking the HVO, and they did not give up their plan to break through to the west and to the sea. And I emphasise once again that there is no single word about the attacks against Serbs, which means in the direction of Banja Luka, the corridor, or Bihac. He said previously that if he had taken Vitez, Hrvatska would have perhaps have stopped supplying Bihac, which never occurred to anybody to do so in Croatia, irrespective of the total incomprehensible behaviour on the part of the BiH Army and the crimes that they had committed, starting with Trusina and onwards. Now let's go on, page 31.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: To a question put by this journalist, or whoever did this, about the role of Alagic in the operation surrounding Vares, he says very clearly that he issued the Vares operation order and that he was given the task to take the 7th Muslim Brigade and embark on the liberation of Vares from that side. One has to understand the fact that the attack on the HVO in Vares, which had been completely calm until then, and I've already spoken about the beginnings of the attack on Vares, and that was a liberation, for this kind of commanders in the BH Army, we were an enemy military and an enemy people. On the following page, he says that the outcomes of the battle were very certain; that they were not afraid that they would not succeed. He goes on to speak about the logistics of the 3rd Corps. He says that there were several logistics centres; that the black market was flourishing; that there were food and ammunitions smuggled; and he says once, in cooperation with the MUP, he tried to put a stop to that, to curb that situation, but that it amounted to conflicts. He says that the situation was very difficult, that they were between a rock and a hard place, and that's why he decided to start trading with the Chetniks in the area of Meokrnje. Therefore, when it comes to the liberation of Bosnia and Herzegovina from the Croats and the HVO, he also cooperated with Chetniks. On page 34 --

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: 3D41-0095, the English translation, and 3D33-0554 is the original.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a reference to the visit by Mr. Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Just a moment. Let me correct the page. 3D33-0354.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Izetbegovic's arrival at the 7th Muslim Brigade and the handing out of the war flag, this illustrates a staged incident that had been neutralised. However, it also says here that some of the power-wielders in Zenica were against Alagic, so one cannot say that all Muslims or all politicians, like, for example, the situation was like in Tuzla, that they agreed to that kind of attitude towards Croats and the HVO. And he says, in his turn, that they were against him because those people in Zenica were involved in the smuggling operations with the Chetniks through Bukovica. And then he speaks about the relations -- the good relations he had with some people. He wanted money to be allocated for the army and whatnot. And then we can go on to the following page.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Which is, in the original, 3D33-0355, and it is also 3D41-0096 for the English version.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter's correction, 0095.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He says that towards the end of the summer, he met Mr. Izetbegovic. He says that he did not know anything about any officers of the BH Army in Sarajevo. He said to Izetbegovic that he, himself, Alagic, had contacts with Bosniaks in Zagreb, and he conveyed greetings to him from Hasan Cengic. And that's the one and the same Hasan Cengic who opposed Izetbegovic in the book written by Filipovic, when he talks about an instance when Izetbegovic could not manage Hasan Cengic and other young Muslims. So Hasan Cengic was in Zagreb, and he was using the logistical centres that the BiH Army had, with the support of the Croatian government and the HV, that he enjoyed in Split, Zagreb and Samobor, to organise the implementation of the plan that the late Mr. Alagic was in the process of implementing. What is important here is that he said to Mr. Alagic, We have to launch an offensive war. When he says that, I claim that he had in mind the HVO, and we're talking about the month of September 1993, when Sefer Halilovic continued the offensive that he had launched already in the month of June, targeting the HVO along the Neretva Valley, and the ultimate goal was to reach the western borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina and thus by doing that to get rid of the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina. In the month of September, their political and military leaderships signed a separate agreement with the Serbs about the future organisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the end of war operations between the BiH Army and the Army of Republika Srpska, in the month of September 1993. Thank you. So much about this book.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, we left it off with the winter months of 1992, and now we are moving to the month of January 1993. For the Trial Chamber and everybody in the courtroom, this is a small file under the title "15 January 1993." Do you wish to say something in general terms or can we start using documents immediately?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I would like to speak in general terms. Here, the Prosecutor, as one of the key elements showing the behaviour of the Croatian Defence Council or, rather, the political leadership of the HZ-HB, speaks about a document that they call a blackmail or an ultimatum, the ultimatum that the HVO sent to the BiH Army on the 15th of January, 1993. This is not correct. I state here that the text of the so-called ultimatum was coordinated in Zagreb on the 13th and 14th of January, 1993. It had been discussed with Mr. Alija Izetbegovic at the Esplanade Hotel in Zagreb. During the talks, at which I was also present, and when it comes to the drafting of the text of this so-called ultimatum, I was also involved in that. There were other people involved; namely, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, Mr. Gojko Susak. And I believe that on one occasion, Mr. Gojko Susak was also in the presence of Lord Owen and Cyrus Vance. The two of them also participated in the talks, and that that document was drafted based on the agreement that had been reached in Geneva between the 1st of January and that time when the delegations returned to Zagreb. And when it comes to the drafting of the so-called ultimatum, I was involved in that together with some other people from the Muslim delegation, in the presence of Mr. Alija Izetbegovic. That document, on the 15th of January, in the morning, I took with me as I went to Mostar, and I handed it over to Mr. Stojic, Mr. Petkovic, and Mr. Prlic. They also signed it and published it. The three of them had nothing whatsoever to do with the document, namely. The only possible minor error occurred because Mr. Izetbegovic agreed that that document would first be publicly broadcast by the minister of defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina; in other words, Mr. Izetbegovic's minister of defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Bozo Rajic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bozo Rajic, Bozo Rajic. Since the fighting around Vakuf was already underway, on that morning, on the 15th of January, 1991 --

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, the year?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: A correction. 1993. I correct myself. I was invited to come to President Tudjman's office, and I can say with 95 percent certainty that Mr. Izetbegovic was also there. And there was a request upon me, and it was more formal than any ordinary request. It was not an order, but it was more than a request. It was still not an order. In any case, it was for me to go to Uskoplje and to calm the situation down. I took the order with me, and when I arrived down there late in the afternoon or in the evening, I don't know when exactly -- actually, when I arrived in Mostar on the 15th of January, 1993, Messrs. Prlic, Stojic and Petkovic heard from me that an agreement had been reached with Mr. Izetbegovic, and I gave them the text. I believe that Mr. Bozo Rajic published that text a day later, because he also had received it as an official document issued by the minister of defence of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which means that he was a joint minister for both the BH Army and the HVO. On the 16th, I went to Uskoplje, and I will dedicate some more time to that later. Mr. Izetbegovic changed his mind about the document, and on the 20th of January, the 20th of January, 1991, he issued an order --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, 20 January 1993. I apologise. Mr. Izetbegovic issued an order by way of which he had annulled the order issued by his defence minister and signed by the people that I mentioned. In the HVO at the time, there was the endless desire to see the conflicts, which could be felt and were ongoing, to come to an end, and that's why we can explain this haste, the haste in which the documents in Mostar were published one day where they were supposed to be; and perhaps I didn't convey the exact instructions that we should wait until the minister made it public, Minister Bozo Rajic, that is, the minister in the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the defence minister, in fact, of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It wasn't an ultimatum at all. Let me repeat, the document came into being on the basis of an agreement. The document wanted to achieve what we want to do achieve from the very beginning, and that is to establish some sort of law and order in the army and thereby to prevent all major problems in the area, in the field. The document didn't do any damage, because on the 20th of January, it was stopped, cancelled, except that we saw once again that, as far as Mr. Izetbegovic was concerned, who changed something he had agreed to previously many times, that he was being controlled by somebody stronger than him. And in this case, according to my information, that person was Haris Silajdzic. And in his statement for this Tribunal about how Silajdzic did this at a meeting which was held at the time, he wrote a statement to this Tribunal. So I have nothing further to add, except to say that we can now look at the transcript, and as far as this agreement is concerned and the creation of this agreement, in conformity with the agreements reached in Geneva, the following persons took part: Cyrus Vance and Lord Owen.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, I have to ask you the question, because according to the transcript it would appear that Haris Silajdzic gave a statement for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Mr. Antun Vrdoljak made a statement for the Defence, who was at the meeting when Mr. Silajdzic, who had just returned from America, exerted pressure on Alija Izetbegovic not to sign an agreement of this kind. And then I suppose that's where he changed his opinion later on, of course with great resistance from his generals, Halilovic and the rest.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: For the record, once again I want to state the numbers of the documents that you referred to. One is P0115 [as interpreted], which is the decision by Dr. Jadranko Prlic; and the second one is P01140, which is an order by the head of the Defence Department of the HZ-HB, Mr. Bruno Stojic; and the third is P01139, which is the order from Brigadier Milivoj Petkovic. I have to repeat the first number, P1155. Thank you, it's correct now. Now, General, linked to the last document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, you addressed the issue of the ultimatum of the 15th of January, 1993. We have the documents before us, and I would like to thank your Defence counsel for having prepared this small binder, which means that we can see all the rest of the documents. On reading this document, we realise that provinces 3, 8 and 10 are being implemented, in military terms. These documents aim at establishing military command, either ABiH ones or HVO ones, depending on which area had been decided upon during the Geneva Conference. That's all very well, but an international conference was held. We understood that you participated in all that very closely. To avoid any problems, couldn't you have suggested to those people that attended the international conference this particular document, in the form of a project document, to see that: A, everybody would agree to it; B, to see whether the states that were -- whose representatives were attending the meeting, the diplomats, like Cyrus Vance or Lord Owen, whether they would agree to this; and, C, whether the opponent or the other side also agreed? If you had everybody's agreement, you could have then circulated this document. Why wasn't this done, and why was it decided to publish all these documents and orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Antonetti, Your Honour, this had been agreed in Geneva, and it was operationalised in Zagreb along with everybody's acquiescence and agreement. When I say "everybody's," then I mean the HVO, on one hand, Mr. Izetbegovic, on the other side, and Cyrus Vance and Lord Owen, on the third side, being the third party. And just to make this quite clear, let's read the minutes once again.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P01158 is the number.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, and it's the 15th of January, in Zagreb, at 1550 hours. The meeting was at Dr. Franjo Tudjman's offices, and Mr. Cyrus Vance was attending, as well as Lord Owen, Alija Izetbegovic, and Mate Boban, and their associates. And look at what Gojko Susak says there. We ought to read them quietly and calmly, and this is what Susak says: "Once again, I'd like to raise a practical question for which I thought that we had understood each other a long time ago." And he goes on to say: "Mr. Izetbegovic, we discussed this in Zagreb, and we discussed it in front of the co-chairman in Geneva," that is to say, Vance and Owen. And he says: "Due to the effectiveness of the war and we are in an unfavorable position anyway, where you have predominantly Muslim forces --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters do not have the text on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And it says in Geneva, this was divided up according to the provinces, so that the Command of the BH Army, even where the HVO forces were, the command should be the HVO. As Izetbegovic quite obviously, because he had a meeting in the evening with Silajdzic, changed his mind, had already changed his mind, he says, and this is Izetbegovic speaking: "Gojko Susak, I can't understand what is being contested here, after all the agreements that we had reached in Geneva, because the joint interest is that we should defend ourselves from a joint enemy, a joint foe." And he goes on to say: "Is this not something that we've already achieved, because an agreement had already been achieved?" And he goes on to say: "I sat together with you in the room --" Yes, I apologise for speaking too quickly. I was sitting in the hotel room, in the hotel here at the Esplanade Hotel, when we made a gentlemen's agreement that you would work on this, and then he goes on to say: "I don't see what is contentious if, in Gornji Vakuf, no matter if there are more Muslims or fewer Croats there, but it is in the territory controlled by the HVO, if orders now coming from Sarajevo are contradictory to orders from Mostar." And he goes on to say: "Well, you're killing yourselves. Then the Serbs do not need to fight you any longer, if that's the case." So since I took part in this, I claim and stand by what I've already said. An agreement had been reached in the matter, and quite obviously -- that is quite obvious because this was discussed in Geneva. And those talks in Geneva would, of course, continue, and on several occasions we kept saying, Let's place the army at least under some sort of control in this way until a final politician solution is found, because with generals of this kind, like Alagic and the rest of them, without a joint command and some sort of -- well, Your Honours, that HVO command was not supposed to be mono-ethnical. There was just the number-one man issuing orders, and it was the second man in command who was supposed to be a Muslim, so this command -- that was the kind of joint command it was, and the BH Army remained the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, with its full establishment, and that was only in order to introduce a minimum of law and order. It wasn't the subordination of one army to another, in the classical sense, for us to be able to speak about any personnel policy, how many soldiers, who was able to replace whom, and things of that kind. You see, you have a problem on the ground, in the field, when there are two commands. There's one unit standing next to another unit, and you don't know how strong each of these are, what the strength of one is and what the strength of the other is, so there is a lack of confidence, generally speaking. According to this agreement, this is a classical form and akin to the system in NATO. The British troops in Iraq are British troops, but there is one commander who coordinates for the Poles over there and the British, one person who coordinates them. The armies, however, retain their entire being and their entire entity. That remains intact. But you have to know who does what.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let me interrupt what you're saying so we can go to the crux of things. There are two pages. The minutes of the meeting is 55 pages' long -- 53 pages -- my colleagues and myself, we'll read the remaining 53 pages, but I don't know what is said afterwards. But Mate Boban, who was there, couldn't he, in fact, and Mr. Vance and Owen say the following: My military experts have prepared orders according to which, as of tomorrow, or as of such and such hour, there will be resubordination between different units between HVO and ABiH, and we are handing you over these orders, these are the orders that are to be sent out a few hours from now, if everybody agrees? Why didn't things follow this course?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Antonetti, that's precisely how it was done. We prepared all that, and Mr. Izetbegovic said, Okay, yeah, that's it, and I will give that to Bozo Rajic to make it public. And I took it with me to Mostar. And it was published a day before by the three people because we wanted to prevent any possible conflicts, and we were in a hurry to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if I understood you correctly, all these documents signed by Mr. Stojic, Petkovic and so forth and so on, were signed and handed over in full agreement with Mr. Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct. The only mistake was that it was first supposed to be made public by Bozo Rajic, and Bozo Rajic, as the defence minister, published it. This document was not submitted here. It should have been also among the documents. And on the 20th of January, Mr. Izetbegovic cancelled the order by his defence minister, Bozo Rajic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But if everyone agreed up until January 20th, this means that it cannot be an ultimatum. When everyone agrees, there can be no ultimatum. Is this a logical inference?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, there is no ultimatum. An agreement is not an ultimatum. This was an agreement that was reached with the Commander-In-Chief, Mr. Izetbegovic, and it was made public by his defence minister, Bozo Rajic. And for reasons that I already stated, and probably the rebellion on the part of his generals because they didn't want that, Mr. Izetbegovic cancelled that on the 20th of January, 1993, without suffering any consequences. There were no consequences for anyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, when you came from Zagreb, did you take with you any orders that were already written or did you just bring with you the meat, so to speak, what has already been agreed?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was written down. I didn't come. It was written down on the paper, well, the agreement that we reached there, all the items, item by item. So I didn't come; it was written down, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: That's what I meant. It was not an order that was already drafted and written down. You started speaking -- or, rather, you said that you would speak about Vakuf a bit later on, when you were speaking about the 15th of January, so perhaps you could now tell the Judges how your stay there proceeded after the 15th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, after I stayed a while, I probably stayed a night in Mostar, and the next day there were some talks about what was going on and so on, in the 16th, in the evening, I reached Rama; on the 16th of January, 1993. I met with Mr. Siljeg, of course, who was the commander of the operational zone, and with Mr. Miro Andric, who was the deputy, Mr. Petkovic's deputy. And one must note here that the problem in Vakuf started a long, long time before that, and it escalated on several occasions, and then the tensions were calmed down and so on. In December 1992, the BH Army had already dug up all of its positions in all the hills around the town of Vakuf and in the Vakuf itself. I have already shown this map, and the English major who was there at the time confirmed its accuracy. And both Mr. Andric and Mr. Siljeg, and on my orders and on my demand, in December 1992 went to a number of meetings with the BH Army Command in Gornji Vakuf to solve this problem, because the line facing the Serbs, as I've shown on the map, was 10, 15 kilometres away, as the crow flies, in the direction of Raducki Kamen, and they covered the line in a very small area, extremely small area, extremely small area, whereas in Vakuf, they had two brigades. And this escalated to such a degree that the HVO commander from Vakuf, Zrinko Tokic, who will testify here, was no longer able to go to his headquarters. For instance, he went to Rama to attend a meeting, and then he was supposed to go to his headquarters in Vakuf, he had to be taken through the town by UNPROFOR. It was quite obvious that the situation was untenable, in military terms, because they had cut off the roads, the main road going through Vakuf and the side roads. There was a small path through Pidris.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: When you say "they," you mean the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the BH Army cut off all the roads, and once all the opportunities to talk were over, they felt, rightly so, that the threat that the BH Army posed by digging the trenches in such a manner, and the position that the HVO found itself was a clear military danger, and that they had to launch a military action to defend themselves against this threat, this danger. And this was launched sometime on the 11th of January. I went there to calm the situation down.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on the 16th of January. I don't have to repeat it so many times. It was the 16th of January, 1993. In the evening, I heard everybody, the information, the arguments of the HVO officers, and I demanded that another round of talks be held with the BH Army in the presence of the English officers from UNPROFOR who were deployed there. There are all those documents that we have seen so many times, with demand that, A, all the trenches be dug over, and that the units from the town -- and so on. It is clear, based on all that, that the BH Army felt that it had the position of strength and that it was a part of its plan to cover the roads towards Bugojno and Central Bosnia, because they obstructed passage through town on all roads; and since the talks did not yield any logical fruit, they decided that the military targets on those hills, so we're talking only about military targets on those hills, something that in military terminology is called "active defence"; so I didn't agree with them, but I didn't have any arguments to argue against them. There was not a single logical argument that I could use to deny them this right.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. At page 86, line 19, the general said "I agreed with them," and it says in the transcript "I didn't agree with them."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, I didn't have the arguments to refute their clean logic that the HVO army -- armed forces should not be brought in a position to be completely blockaded in Vakuf, with the passage to Bugojno, with the Chetniks on the other side, because the BH Army had already left the lines facing the Chetniks. This is inadmissible. The talks up there were going on, the tripartite talks; BH Army, HVO, and the English, they also took part in it. The action was launched. It was a clean military action, and I contacted on the 18th or 19th already, I don't know, because again, Your Honours, the delegations that were in Zagreb went back to Geneva. And General Petkovic also travelled to Geneva, and I, of course, was not able to establish any direct links with Geneva; so I called Susak, asking me to put me in touch with Boban, and Petkovic, and whoever else it was I talked to, I really don't know, and how this whole complicated communication went on, to tell them what was going on. And I asked that the commanders who were in Geneva, General Petkovic and General Halilovic - I think that he was also in Geneva at that time, I'm not sure - that orders be issued for the conflict to stop, but with the proviso that there are positions that should be removed from the mountains and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, we will stop your testimony now, because we only have a few minutes left. This is an important issue, and I'm sure that you will continue with this next week. We are now around the 18th and 19th of January, 1993, and you are giving us a chronological testimony, so I'm sure that we will come back to this issue next week. All in all, I believe that you must have about ten hours left. I don't have the exact time left. If we need to continue the week after next week, well, that's a possibility, if you haven't finished yet. But altogether, we are counting on the 36 hours that you asked for, and you've used up 26 hours so far, so you have 10 left. We'll reconvene on Monday at 2.15 p.m. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 25th day of May, 2009, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: [The Accused Prlic and Coric not present]
--- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.44 p.m.,
